items.title: 61521_David Albert Francis oral history interview
items.q: and that's where I met them, in Washington

ctx.x: Well, that's quite true, they might think that, and in some cases, that might be true, but there was also another element of it, too, because we had no record companies of our own, as black musicians, and we worked for other companies, and it was kind of hard, kind of difficult for us to get into that end of the business.

That's another thing I tried to do, and I don't know whether you know it or not, but I started out with Atlantic Records when they were in a loft on 54th Street and 8th Avenue. The company was owned at that time by Herb Abramson and his wife, Miriam -- and Ahmet Ertegun Nesuhi, and his brother, Lester, was in Washington -- they were just two young European boys who were living in Washington, because their father was the Ambassador or something from Turkey, and they were interested in rhythm-and-blues and jazz --…

after that -- he came in later on. But I started out with Atlantic Records, and I tried to get -- after I saw what was happening, that Atlantic was making all this money with these hits that they had, songs on the charts and everything, which was another thing that was just being started -- by Variety and the different magazines, of putting songs on charts.
